etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English arest (noun) and aresten (verb), from Old French areste (noun) and arester (“to stay, stop”, verb), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”), equivalent to ad- +‎ rest. Compare French arrêter (“to stop”).

definitions.definition: A check, stop, an act or instance of arresting something.
The condition of being stopped, standstill.
(law) The process of arresting a criminal, suspect etc.
A confinement, detention, as after an arrest.
A device to physically arrest motion.
(nautical) The judicial detention of a ship to secure a financial claim against its operators.
(obsolete) Any seizure by power, physical or otherwise.

quote.citation: 1651–1653, Jer[emy] Taylor, ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΣ [Eniautos]. A Course of Sermons for All the Sundays of the Year. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Richard Royston […], published 1655, →OCLC:
quote.text: The sad stories of fire from heaven, the burning of his sheep, etc.,  […]  were sad arrests to his troubled spirit.

definitions.definition: (farriery) A scurfiness of the back part of the hind leg of a horse[1]
(obsolete, transitive) To stop the motion of (a person, animal, or body part). [14th–19th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act II, scene vii:
quote.text: An vncouth paine torments my grieued ſoule,And death arreſts the organe of my voyce.

quote.citation: 1708, [John Philips], “Book I”, in Cyder. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 11:
quote.text: Nor could her virtues, nor repeated vows Of thousand lovers, the relentless hand Of Death arrest;

quote.citation: 1952, Doris Lessing, Martha Quest, Panther, published 1974, page 86:
quote.text: Mr. Van Rensberg broke the spell by arresting Martha as she trailed past him on Billy's arm, by pointing his pipestem at her and saying, ‘Hey, Matty, come here a minute.’
A white Starre […] whiche to every mans sighte did lighte and arrest apon the Standard of Albry.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To stop or slow (a process, course etc.). [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1994, Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom: The Autobiography of Nelson Mandela, London: Abacus, published 2010, page 707:
quote.text: To try to arrest the spiral of violence, I contacted Chief Buthelezi to arrange a meeting.

quote.citation: 1997: Chris Horrocks, Introducing Foucault, page 69 (Totem Books, Icon Books; →ISBN
quote.text: Knowledge replaced universal resemblance with finite differences. History was arrested and turned into tables …Western reason had entered the age of judgement.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To seize (someone) with the authority of the law; to take into legal custody. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: I arrest thee of high treason.

quote.citation: 1941, George Orwell, The Lion and the Unicorn, Pt. I:
quote.text: The policeman who arrests the "Red" does not understand the theories the "Red" is preaching; if he did, his own position as bodyguard of the monied class might seem less pleasant to him.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To catch the attention of. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 1919: P. G. Wodehouse, My Man Jeeves:
quote.text: There is something about this picture—something bold and vigorous, which arrests the attention. I feel sure it would be highly popular.

quote.citation: 2004, Euan A. Ashley, Josef Niebauer, Cardiology Explained, page 66:
quote.text: Realizing the mistake immediately from the outline of the RCA on the fluoroscope screen, he rapidly removed the catheter – just as his patient arrested.
